# Release-trust golden vectors

The behaviour of the release trust gates, written down as data. They were generated from
the Go updater (`control-plane/internal/updater`, #356, RH06 decision A3), so its Rust
port in the recovery actor (`node-agent/crates/quasar-recovery`, module `trust`) could be
held to the same answers. The Go updater retired with #367; its answers are frozen here,
and these files are now the definition of the behaviour.

- Rust: `every_trust_vector_passes_against_the_rust_port` in
  `node-agent/crates/quasar-recovery/src/trust/vector_tests.rs` (`make test-rust`).

The runner fails on a file or a `kind` it does not know, or a kind that is missing, runs
every vector in every file, and checks that the count it ran equals the count on disk. A
vector it does not run is therefore a failing test, not a silent gap.

## Where the vectors come from

Every expectation is the Go updater's own output for the inputs, as generated by its case
table (`trustvectors_cases_test.go`, in git history before #367). Where a case came from
one of the Go updater's tests, its `source` names that file and test (`go:…`); the files
are gone, the provenance stays. `added:` cases pin a rule those tests exercised only
implicitly (check order, a boundary, a Go `encoding/json` / `net/url` / `encoding/base64`
quirk the port must reproduce).

A change to a trust rule is now a change to these files and the Rust port together, and
goes through the same security review as the port did: a vector is never edited to make a
failing port green.

Messages are pinned exactly, except where Go embedded text from a library (a JSON syntax
error, a transport error, a `net/netip` error); there the part the updater authored is
pinned as `message_prefix` / `error_prefix`.

## Files

| file | kind | what it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `admit.json` | `admit` | `Plan`'s request gates (uuid, single flight, closed component table, image, digest, namespace allowlist, in that order) and the ADR 0003 signature gate. `fetch` vectors gather evidence the way the updater's server does. `caller: agent` vectors pin the agent-socket guard (architecture §5.2) and the recovery actor accepting a request that names itself (amendment 14; the updater never does), neither of which the caller-less Go updater has: Go is held to `expect_without_caller_guard`, the port to both. A `caller: control_plane` vector carries `expect_without_caller_guard` only where the port admits what Go refuses (the control socket naming the recovery actor together with the control plane, ADR 0008 rule A): Go is held to it, the port to `expect`. |
| `verify_signature.json` | `verify_signature` | `VerifyManifestSignature`: the detached document decoded exactly as Go decodes it, any entry under any trusted key, key rotation. |
| `evidence.json` | `evidence` | How HTTP outcomes become `signed` / `absent` / `fetch_error`. Only a 404 on the signature asset is an absence. A `fetch` with `asset_format: 2` is about the format-2 pair (`platform-release-manifest.v2.json` and its `.sig`) the recovery actor reads (control-api.md amendment 14); without it, the updater's format-1 pair. Each runner fetches the pair the vector names, and the actor's production path uses the format-2 pair. |
| `evidence_gate.json` | `evidence_gate` | Whether a request's assets are fetched at all. |
| `config.json` | `config` | The operator knobs: signature mode, trusted keys, allowed namespaces, manifest base URL. |
| `redirect.json` | `redirect` | The fetch's redirect policy. |

Byte strings are `{"text": ...}` (exact UTF-8), `{"base64": ...}`, or
`{"segments": [{"text": ..., "count": n}]}` for large or deeply nested inputs.
URLs live under `https://releases.example.invalid`.

## Keys

No key material is committed. A
vector names a key by label (`"public_key_of": "release-2026"`, or
`{public_key_of:release-2026}` inside a trusted-key list), and the runner derives it:
the ed25519 seed is SHA-256 of the fixed prefix `KEY_SEED_PREFIX` (vector_tests.rs) followed by
the label. These keys are **public by construction** — anyone can recompute the private
half — so they are test keys only. Never put one in `QUASAR_UPDATER_TRUSTED_KEYS`.

## Where the Rust fetch differs from Go's

The vectors pin the decisions; the HTTPS client under them (`trust::https`) was held to
the Go updater's `signature_source.go` on `http.DefaultTransport` by its own tests. Where
it cannot match Go it refuses, so each difference can only turn a Go success into a
`signature_invalid`, never into an unverified apply. Two are documented limits of an owned
install (`docs/configuration.md` "Release trust"), decided at the updater's retirement
(#367):

- **Proxies.** The fetch has no proxy client: a request that `HTTPS_PROXY` (with
  `NO_PROXY`) would route through a proxy is refused. A machine that reaches the release
  host only through a proxy cannot run `verify` or `require`; it runs `off` (ADR 0001
  trust: the pinned digest and the namespace allowlist).
- **Trust roots.** The client uses webpki-roots (Mozilla's set) and ignores
  `SSL_CERT_FILE` / `SSL_CERT_DIR`, so a mirror behind a private CA fails closed. Point
  `QUASAR_UPDATER_MANIFEST_BASE_URL` at a host with a publicly trusted certificate.

Also different, and refusing the same way: a non-ASCII mirror host (no IDNA), HTTP/2
(not offered), and connection reuse (none). Refusal and error message text follows Go's
where it can; only the prefix Go authored is pinned.
